title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
author: Rob Davis
content:
When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the
state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to
address a [story ProPublica published that
morning](https://www.propublica.org/article/oregon-housing-director-husband-
conflict).

The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed
her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities
develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she
notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a
governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.

Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing
subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be
clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my
household income.”

Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the
council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that
Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state
funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s
employer is helping to develop.

Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5
million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from
Bell’s agency.

JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites,
will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if
the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.

A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas
County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months
after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas
County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the
new records show.

Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that
if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward,
“no fee shall be due” to the firm.

JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not
worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to
Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that
is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de
Gorgue.

Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a
statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and
compliance with state law.”

“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to
influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear,
I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not
received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”

Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a
homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor,
has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing
and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars
to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.

Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who
teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the
governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions
about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.

“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows
who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look
like she’s trying to conceal this.”

De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in
development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action
to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any
advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications
were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.

“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which
we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de
Gorgue said.

Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a
consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.

Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she
amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner
as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before
that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a
developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not
its name.)

Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion
about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That
evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in
response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary
review is ongoing.

ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county
contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s
public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50
to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged
$364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.

Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built,
it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to
come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay
will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even
larger subsidy.

ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing
agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and
said the state agency director was receptive to talking further.

The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had
with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another
department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of
urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018
voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional
government.

Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental
housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical”
to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding
for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not
respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment.

Behind the Aloha 209th discussion was the way that Oregon awards its housing
subsidies. Since 2024, Oregon has given the money on a first-come, first-
served basis. When funding runs out, Bell’s agency places applications on a
waitlist in the order received.

Bell spoke with Washington County officials about Aloha 209th during a
45-minute Zoom meeting in August, records show. Internal notes summarizing the
conversation say that the county would send an updated report to the state
agency to “inform movement of 209.” The summary said the groups involved would
have a follow-up conversation about the project.

Bell went on to discuss the project with regional government officials in
early September. About two weeks before the meeting, she emailed her deputy
with two possible ways to get the project funded: a legislative “carve-out” or
Metro consolidating its subsidies so it could fully pay for the project. “I
want to do everything we can to help the metro projects be successful and the
resources, like ours, are nearly depleted,” Bell wrote. She acknowledged that
Metro might not find the solution appealing.

Bell told ProPublica that she met with Metro and Washington County at the
other agencies’ request. She said her agency “does not have and is not
pursuing a ‘legislative carve out’ for any project.”

“My approach is to listen to partners’ concerns and explain our funding
process,” she said in an email. “I have no role in deciding whether projects
should receive funding as part of this process, and I do not advocate for
individual projects. Characterizing these routine discussions and legitimate
concerns as something improper fundamentally misrepresents their purpose and
context.”

A spokesperson for Washington County’s housing authority told ProPublica that
Bell did not make any commitment to alter the prioritization of Aloha 209th.
Another Washington County spokesperson said the August meeting with Bell was
mainly focused on the housing authority’s desire for “clearer criteria” for
how projects on the state’s waitlist get funded.

A Metro spokesperson said the regional agency requested the September meeting
with a goal “for the two agencies to strengthen our working relationship and
coordination.”

“Metro does not, and did not, advocate for any specific project,” the
spokesperson said. “We clearly indicated this at the meeting and in writing
ahead of the meeting.” The agency has advocated for a group of remaining
projects, including Aloha 209th, to get money so Metro can fulfill commitments
made as part of its affordable housing bond, the spokesperson said.

Oregon’s Government Ethics Commission has until early December to complete its
preliminary review of the complaint over Bell’s financial disclosure, which
will help the agency decide whether to open a full investigation.

Bell said she will “continue to remain responsive to the Ethics Commission” as
it completes its examination.

Kotek’s office, provided with a list of ProPublica’s latest findings, said in
a statement that the governor “holds all agency leadership to consistent and
high ethical standards” and that her office “is closely following” the ethics
panel’s review.
